title: Most Frequently Tested Topics
tagline: Year 4 — Building a priority list of topics from your own mock data and the standard syllabus, with no invented frequency claims

introduction.overview: Which topics are tested most often depends on the employer and changes every year, and there is no reliable public count of question frequency. Rather than repeat claims about "top topics", this chapter teaches you to build your own priority list: take the standard syllabus areas, record how often each appears in the mocks and practice papers you take, record your accuracy in each, and rank them by expected marks gained per hour of study. The result is a personal priority list that updates as you practise. The figures in this chapter's examples are illustrative and not real test statistics.
introduction.placementRelevance: A data-driven priority list focuses limited study hours where they earn the most marks.
introduction.realWorldContext: Prioritising work by expected return is a basic planning skill.

learningObjectives: Record topic frequency from your own mocks
Estimate marks gained per hour of study

requiredTopics: Common Traps and How to Avoid Them
prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Expected gain = frequency × (target accuracy − current accuracy). Priority = gain ÷ hours needed.

coreDefinitions: Frequency: how many times a topic appears in your mocks.
Accuracy: correct ÷ attempted in the topic.
Gap: target accuracy minus current accuracy.
Expected gain: marks you can add by closing the gap.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Study where there is both frequent testing and a big gap.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Tabulate frequency and accuracy, compute gain, divide by hours, rank.

mainNarrative: Over 5 mocks suppose percentage questions appeared 40 times and you got 28 right: accuracy 70%. With a 90% target the gap is 20 points, so expected gain over the same number of questions is 40 × 0.2 = 8 marks.
Seating puzzles appeared 20 times with 8 right: accuracy 40%, gap 50 points, expected gain 10 marks.
If closing the percentage gap takes 8 hours and the seating gap 20 hours, priorities are 1.0 and 0.5 marks per hour: do percentages first.
Re-rank after each mock because the accuracy changes.
Mark any claim about "most tested topics" that you cannot verify as hearsay.

deepDiveAspects.title: Sample size
deepDiveAspects.content: With few questions in a topic the accuracy estimate is noisy; combine with practice sets.

deepDiveAspects.title: Core topics
deepDiveAspects.content: Foundational topics (percentages, ratios, averages) support many others and are worth studying regardless.
